<reason>Side B (PRO) won a competitive but clear debate. Both sides were disciplined and grounded. CON's strongest live route was the litigation-driven slippery slope (Canada's lines struck down as discriminatory), but PRO answered it with the Oregon counterexample and the point that Canada's expansion flowed from a specific Charter framing, and CON's rejoinder that Oregon "hasn't finished the litigation" was assertion rather than evidence — the counterexample survived. CON's other big route, the certainty of documented harms vs a hypothetical patient, was blunted when PRO noted the Oregon "burden" survey line shows patient worries, not coercion, and never fully neutralized PRO's central comparison: safeguarded law vs an unregulated status quo where violent suicide, secret family assistance, and covert pressure already occur with no witnesses. CON never defended those status quo harms beyond a weak claim that criminal families have "nowhere to hide," which gets the deterrence logic backwards. PRO answered both pressure questions directly (A1/A2 labels, structural safeguards parallel to ordinary capacity assessment), while PRO's pressure questions exposed that CON had no positive offer for the ALS patient beyond sedation — and PRO's closing that sedation is "a substitution, not a response" landed cleanly. Both sides had one clipped turn, so execution costs roughly cancel. PRO's comparative weighing (certain vs speculative harm, real person vs unnamed future patients) made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was PRO's closing [B5.1]–[B5.3] against CON's A4.3 answer: when CON offered the ALS patient palliative sedation and treatment refusal as full protection, PRO reframed sedation-to-unconsciousness as overriding her stated choice rather than honoring it, and paired it with the observation that CON's slope theory required Oregon's twenty-five-year counterexample to fall — which CON never made fall.</best_rebuttal>
